description: We are a team of Systems Engineering students from the Universidad Nacional de Villa Mercedes. We are passionate about programming, software development, and building innovative projects designed to support our community and promote sustainability
summary:
OrbitAR is an interactive, educational video game that invites secondary school students to become architects of a space mission. By selecting scientific objectives, designing their own spacecraft, and making strategic decisions during the launch, players gain hands-on experience with the challenges and opportunities of the aerospace sector.
Designed for virtual workshops and accessible educational experiences, the project aims to remove the geographical barriers that often limit access to career guidance and science outreach activities. Through an engaging, immersive experience, students discover how various academic disciplines come together to enable major breakthroughs in space exploration—and how they, too, can contribute to the solutions that will shape the future.
details:
The Problem: The Vocational Gap and STEM Talent Shortage

Argentina faces a strategic challenge: the growing demand for professionals in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) contrasts with the low number of young people choosing and completing degrees in these disciplines

This situation is deepened by two main factors:

  • Shortage of professionals in strategic sectors: The current training of specialists is insufficient to meet the needs of technological, scientific, and engineering industries that drive economic development and innovation.
  • Misinformation and cultural barriers: Many students are unaware of the academic and job opportunities available in their own region. Added to this are persistent prejudices about STEM careers, which are frequently perceived as overly difficult, inaccessible, or disconnected from everyday reality.

Our Solution: Bringing STEM Thinking Closer in an Accessible and Meaningful Way.

OrbitAR proposes a game-based learning experience to demonstrate that science and engineering are not fields reserved for a select few, but rather creative tools for solving real-world problems.

Through challenges inspired by space missions, players put planning, analysis, design, and decision-making skills into practice. Every action within the game reflects processes used by professionals across various scientific and technological disciplines.

The goal is to spark curiosity, build confidence in one's own abilities, and offer a first look into the academic and career paths linked to the STEM ecosystem.

Project Objectives

General Objective: Promote young people's interest in science, technology, and space exploration through OrbitAR, an interactive experience that teaches about the design, planning, and development of space missions. 

Objetivos específicos:

  1. Identify and understand the stages of a space mission: Learn how a mission is planned, from selecting scientific objectives to designing the spacecraft, choosing its components, and preparing for launch.
  2. Apply scientific and technological knowledge through experimentation: Use basic aerospace concepts in physics, telecommunications, and engineering to build and assemble a space vehicle, understanding the function of each part and how they interact..
  3. Develop problem-solving and teamwork skills: Foster logical thinking, creativity, and decision-making through interactive challenges that allow players to analyze situations, find solutions, and learn about the different careers and professions linked to the aerospace industry.

Learning Through Experimentation

One of the most important aspects of OrbitAR is that learning is not limited to just reading information. We want students to learn by experimenting. For example, if a spacecraft has too much mass or lacks the appropriate components, the chances of completing the mission may decrease. This allows players to understand why every decision matters and how small changes can affect an outcome. Additionally, every component and challenge will include educational information explaining how it works and its connection to different scientific fields.

Accessibility and Educational Inclusion

The project is designed so that any student can participate, regardless of their geographic location or prior knowledge of space. Being a digital experience, we aim for it to be usable across different devices without requiring advanced knowledge to start playing. We also want the content to be easy to understand, using visual explanations, examples, and hands-on activities that allow for progressive learning.

How Does the Game Work?

When starting the game, players create a new campaign or select a saved one. Upon starting a new campaign, a robot assistant greets the player and explains the function of each section of the game.

Players have access to Planet Earth, the Moon, and Planet Mars. Selecting one reveals graphs of main and secondary missions. To unlock the other levels, players must complete Earth's main mission graph.

When completing a mission, players receive rewards such as money, science points, and even new missions.

OrbitAR’s gameplay is based on a turn-based system. Each turn represents one month; meaning that every time the user advances a turn, one month passes in the game. The user has a monthly budget (money and science points) received upon advancing to the next turn.

Main missions are mandatory to progress in the game and have a specific deadline. Completing them yields rewards (more money and science points).

Secondary missions are optional; they can be completed at the player's convenience (taking into account the main mission's deadline and/or current budget).

When choosing a mission, the game specifies the requirements for the spacecraft to be launched and the duration of the expedition. Starting the mission takes the player to the workshop to build the required spacecraft.

The probability of success is determined by the components chosen for the spacecraft, the season of the year, among other factors.*¹

In the workshop, players find the basic parts needed to build something "basic," while other components are unlocked by purchasing them with research points in the Development section.

Once all necessary components are placed to build a spacecraft, the mission can be launched, deducting the cost of the components from the budget.

Upon finishing missions, as mentioned earlier, players earn money and science points. These science points can be used in the Development section to unlock new, required components for future missions

How Did We Build It?

To create OrbitAR, we brainstormed and discussed the given prompt, looking at how we could solve the challenge with the resources and knowledge we had. We had a clear idea: an interactive game that sparks interest and imparts knowledge regarding space technology and telecommunications. Alongside that idea, we introduced the core problem: the national shortage of professionals in those sectors. With these two key concepts, we began designing how the game would work and what tools we would use.

We divided the work as follows: one person focused on scientific research, another on sketches and application design, another on writing the report, and two people dedicated to application development, covering both front-end and back-end. Even so, every team member contributed a bit to each area.

For application development, we used HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript as our core technologies for the Front-End implementation. Furthermore, we used Node.js as the runtime environment for development tools and Vite 8 to manage the development server and application build. Finally, we incorporated Material Symbols to provide the icons used in the graphical interface

Expected Impact

We hope OrbitAR becomes an educational tool that brings space exploration closer to new generations. Our purpose is not only to teach about space, but to show that behind every scientific breakthrough, there are people who started out learning, experimenting, and developing new ideas. We aim for students to discover their interests, recognize their capabilities, and consider new academic and professional training opportunities.

Future Vision

  • Spacesuit Development: In future stages of the project, we aim to incorporate the design and development of spacesuits once players reach the most advanced missions. Players will have to select different materials and components to protect astronauts from the extreme conditions of space, taking into account factors such as temperature, pressure, oxygen, and mobility. This will introduce knowledge related to biology, physics, chemistry, and materials engineering. 
  • *¹ Better Use of Resources: To start, as this is a beta project, we will only begin with basic variables for mission success probability—for example, spacecraft/satellite mass, season of the year, etc. Once the project progresses and different blueprints for spacecraft and satellite parts are completed, we will begin developing more variables, making the game more realistic and educational.
  • Biomining: We will focus on this area once players have progressed through missions on Earth and the Moon. Afterward, we will introduce missions on Mars focused on using microorganisms (such as bacteria and fungi) to extract metals and minerals, which will be sold in exchange for money and science points. We will also add information from various research areas so players can investigate how to use these organisms, manage the obtained resources, and understand their potential applications in future space missions—all while encouraging students to learn about biotechnology and sparking their interest in the field.
